misconceptions.description: Adding themes, animations, and clip art before the slide has a clear single message
misconceptions.trigger: learner spends time on transitions while three slides still carry no headline claim
misconceptions.feedback: Write the one-sentence headline for each slide first; decorate only after every slide states its point.

misconceptions.description: Treating a wall of bullet points as if it were slide structure
misconceptions.trigger: learner pastes a paragraph as eight bullets with no hierarchy or takeaway
misconceptions.feedback: Replace the bullet dump with one assertion headline plus at most three supporting points.

misconceptions.description: Believing a polished theme proves the deck is well structured
misconceptions.trigger: learner says the deck is done because the template looks consistent
misconceptions.feedback: Structure is the arc of headlines, not the theme. Read the headlines alone and check they tell the story.

misconceptions.description: Equating fewer words with a structured slide, as if cutting the title to a short topic word were the same as making it an assertion.
misconceptions.trigger: learner cuts a title down to a three-word topic label and calls the slide structured
misconceptions.feedback: A short title is not the goal; a claim is. 'Results' is shorter than the assertion, but it states no point a reader could agree or disagree with. Structure means the title asserts the finding and the bullets prove it, at any length.

misconceptions.description: Accepting an AI or template redesign that demotes the headline claim to a small caption while centering a beautiful image.
misconceptions.trigger: learner accepts a redesign that centers an image and shrinks or buries the assertion
misconceptions.feedback: Before accepting a redesign, check what happened to the claim. A layout that turns your assertion into a caption has traded the argument for decoration; reject or modify the suggestion so the claim stays the headline.
